set1.q: Which statement about the transmission of genital herpes is accurate?
opts: It spreads mainly by respiratory droplets

Respiratory droplets, with fluid from active skin lesions, spread varicella zoster virus, the cause of chickenpox. Herpes simplex virus type 2 spreads by direct contact with secretions, even without visible lesions.
It spreads mainly through blood products

Minute amounts of blood and blood products transmit hepatitis B virus. Genital herpes spreads by direct contact with secretions containing herpes simplex virus type 2, sometimes with no lesions visible.
It can spread without visible lesions

Correct. Herpes simplex spreads by direct exposure to secretions containing the virus. Active lesions are the most significant source, but genital herpes can be transmitted in the absence of lesions, so herpes simplex virus type 2 can spread without visible lesions.
It needs visible active lesions to spread

Active lesions are the most significant source, but they are not required: genital herpes can be transmitted in the absence of lesions. That is why a partner with no visible sores can still pass herpes simplex virus type 2.

set1.q: Most DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) viruses are budded off which part of the host cell?
opts: The cytoplasm
Multiplying in and release from the cytoplasm describes most RNA (ribonucleic acid) viruses. Most DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) viruses are budded off the nucleus.
The cell wall
A cell wall is the bacterial layer that phage lysozyme breaches and bursts. Animal cells are drawn with a cell membrane, and most DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) viruses are budded off the nucleus.
An endocytic vesicle

An endocytic vesicle is how a virus enters: it is engulfed into a vesicle by endocytosis at penetration. Most DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) viruses are budded off the nucleus. To tell them apart: entry, not exit.
The nucleus
Correct. Most DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) viruses are budded off the nucleus, while most RNA (ribonucleic acid) viruses multiply in and are released from the cytoplasm.

set1.q: How does roseola from human herpesvirus 6 typically unfold in a baby?
opts: Vesicles with malaise and fever
Fluid-filled vesicles with malaise and fever are chickenpox, the primary varicella zoster infection. Roseola gives a faint maculopapular rash after the fever, not vesicles.
Fever first, then a faint rash

Correct. Roseola is an acute febrile disease of babies 2 to 12 months old: it begins with fever, followed by a faint maculopapular rash, and is usually self-limited. Adults infected with human herpesvirus 6 may instead get mono-like symptoms, lymphadenopathy and hepatitis.
A faint rash first, then fever
This reverses the order. Roseola begins with fever, and the faint maculopapular rash follows: an acute febrile disease followed by rash.
A cheek rash with low fever
A low-grade fever with a rash on the cheeks, the slapped face, is fifth disease from parvovirus B19. Roseola starts with fever and is followed by a faint maculopapular rash.

set1.q: How do humans usually catch orf virus?
opts: Inhaling airborne saliva
Inhaled airborne saliva spreads smallpox from person to person. Orf virus is caught from sheep and goats by people who feed, shear or are bitten by them.
Keeping pet prairie dogs
Pet prairie dogs carried mpox to people in a United States outbreak. Orf virus is a parapox virus of sheep and goats, passed to people who feed, shear or are bitten by the animals.
Handling sheep and goats

Correct. Orf virus is a parapox virus mainly of ruminant animals, sheep and goats, in which it causes sores on the mouth. People catch it by handling the animals: feeding, shearing and bites. It is more serious in the immunocompromised.
Handling rodent-hunting cats
Handling cats that interacted with rodents is how people catch cowpox. Orf virus comes from ruminants, sheep and goats, through feeding, shearing and bites.

set1.q: How does latent herpesvirus DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) differ from a phage prophage?
opts: It is detectable in tissue

Latent virus is generally not detectable; being detectable in tissue marks chronic infection. The episome differs from a prophage in not being integrated. To tell them apart: detectability is the chronic-versus-latent divider, not the prophage comparison.
It is not integrated

Correct. A prophage is phage DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) integrated into the bacterial chromosome. Latent herpesvirus DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) is an episome, in the nucleus but not integrated, though both lie dormant and can later reactivate into active virus production.
It lies in the cytoplasm

The latent herpesvirus episome sits in the nucleus, not the cytoplasm. Its difference from a prophage is that it is not integrated into the host chromosome. To tell them apart: both the episome and the prophage sit with the host genetic material; only one is joined to it.
It can never reactivate

Latent herpesvirus can reactivate and cause recurrent infection, much as a prophage can be induced. The difference is that the episome is not integrated into the chromosome. To tell them apart: dormant is not dead.

set1.q: Which skin condition may be a risk factor for molluscum contagiosum, through breaks in the skin?
opts: Cold sores

Cold sores, or fever blisters, are lesions of herpes simplex virus type 1 near the lips, not a risk factor for molluscum contagiosum. The condition that may raise the risk, through breaks in the skin, is atopic dermatitis.
Shingles

Shingles is reactivated varicella zoster virus with vesicles along a dermatome; it is a disease, not a risk factor named for molluscum contagiosum. Atopic dermatitis, by breaking the skin, may be the risk factor.
Atopic dermatitis

Correct. Atopic dermatitis may be a risk factor for molluscum contagiosum because of the breaks it leaves in the skin. The virus spreads by direct contact and fomites and causes small, smooth, waxy lesions in the genital area and on the thighs.
Plantar warts

Plantar warts are deep, painful warts on the soles of the feet caused by human papillomavirus; they are a disease of their own, not a risk factor named for molluscum. The risk factor is atopic dermatitis, through breaks in the skin.

set1.q: Which stimulus can trigger a recurrence of a latent herpes simplex virus type 1 infection?
opts: Eating salt-cured foods

Eating salt-cured foods is a risk factor for nasopharyngeal carcinoma, a tumor linked to Epstein-Barr virus. Herpes simplex recurrences follow fever, ultraviolet radiation, stress or mechanical injury.
Handling sheep or goats

Handling sheep or goats, by feeding, shearing or bites, passes orf virus, a parapoxvirus, to humans. It is a new infection, not a trigger for latent herpes simplex, which reactivates with fever, ultraviolet light, stress or injury.
Coinfection with malaria

Chronic coinfection with malaria may be associated with Burkitt lymphoma, an Epstein-Barr virus tumor in central African children. The listed triggers for herpes simplex recurrence are fever, ultraviolet radiation, stress and mechanical injury.
Ultraviolet radiation

Correct. Recurrent herpes simplex infection is triggered by stimuli such as fever, ultraviolet radiation, stress and mechanical injury. Newly formed viruses then migrate from the ganglion to the body surface and produce a local skin or membrane lesion, such as a cold sore.

set1.q: A newborn's mother is infected with hepatitis B virus. What gives the newborn passive immunization?
opts: Delivery by cesarean section

Delivery by cesarean section is the step taken when a mother has a herpes simplex outbreak at the time of birth. For hepatitis B the newborn is passively immunized with hepatitis B immune globulin (HBIG).
An adeno-associated virus vector

Adeno-associated virus is a gene therapy vector, approved for lipoprotein lipase deficiency; it gives no immunity to hepatitis B. Passive immunization of the newborn uses hepatitis B immune globulin (HBIG).
Hepatitis B immune globulin (HBIG)

Correct. Passive immunization with hepatitis B immune globulin (HBIG) is given to people exposed or possibly exposed, including neonates born to infected mothers and health care workers. Vaccination, the primary prevention, is active immunity and is encouraged for all newborns.
The yeast-derived surface antigen vaccine

The vaccine from surface antigen cloned in yeast gives ACTIVE immunity and is encouraged for all newborns, but the question asks for passive protection. That is hepatitis B immune globulin (HBIG), given to neonates of infected mothers.

set1.q: At the end of the phage lytic cycle, how are the new virions released?
opts: Lysozyme bursts the wall

Correct. Release is the last lytic step: viral lysozyme causes the host cell wall to burst, freeing the new virions and destroying the host cell. Destruction of the host cell is one of the defining features of the lytic cycle.
Extrusion without lysis

Extrusion without lysis is the chronic cycle of filamentous phages: virions leave continuously and the host only grows more slowly. The lytic cycle ends with viral lysozyme bursting the wall and killing the host.
Budding off the membrane

Budding is how animal viruses leave, which may give them an envelope. A phage in the lytic cycle frees its virions when viral lysozyme bursts the bacterial cell wall. To tell them apart: budding is the animal virus exit; lysozyme bursting is the phage exit.
Induction by a shock
A shock induces a prophage to leave the bacterial chromosome and start a lytic cycle; it begins the cycle, it does not release virions. Release happens when viral lysozyme bursts the cell wall.

set1.q: Mpox virus enters the body through broken skin, mucous membranes, or which other route?
opts: The respiratory tract

Correct. Mpox virus enters through broken skin, the respiratory tract or mucous membranes, by contact with infected animals or humans, their body fluids, or fomites. Fever, aches, chills, swollen lymph nodes and exhaustion follow, then the rash.
Intact skin
The skin route needs a break: mpox virus enters through BROKEN skin, along with the respiratory tract and mucous membranes. Intact skin is not listed as a way in.
The placenta

Crossing the placenta to cause developmental defects is the route of teratogenic viruses such as rubella and cytomegalovirus. Mpox virus enters through broken skin, mucous membranes and the respiratory tract.
The fifth cranial nerve
Herpes simplex virus type 1 enters the fifth cranial nerve and lies latent in the trigeminal ganglion. Mpox virus gets into the body through broken skin, mucous membranes and the respiratory tract.

set1.io: 1 — Recall the steps of DNA virus replication.
set1.q: Adeno-associated virus is a defective parvovirus. What does it need to replicate in a host cell?
opts: Co-infection with adenovirus

Correct. Adeno-associated virus is a defective parvovirus: it cannot replicate in the host cell without adenovirus. By itself it is not known to cause disease, although co-infection with an adenovirus that causes hepatitis may make that infection more severe.
Co-infection with hepatitis B virus
Hepatitis B virus is the partner of hepatitis D, the delta agent, whose co-infection worsens severe hepatitis B. Adeno-associated virus depends on adenovirus to replicate.
Co-infection with BK polyomavirus
BK polyomavirus lies dormant in the kidney and the lining of the ureters and bladder. Adeno-associated virus, a defective parvovirus, cannot replicate without adenovirus.
A bacterial host cell
Bacterial host cells are what bacteriophages infect. As a defective parvovirus, adeno-associated virus needs adenovirus present to replicate.

set1.q: How is parvovirus B19 transmitted?
opts: Droplet infection

Correct. Parvovirus B19 spreads by droplet infection. It causes fifth disease in children, with a slapped-face rash and low-grade fever, hydrops fetalis when passed to a fetus, and polyarthropathy in adults.
Blood or serum contact
Contact with blood or serum, plus sexual contact, is the route of hepatitis B virus. Parvovirus B19, the cause of the slapped-face rash of fifth disease, spreads by droplet infection.
Direct skin contact
Direct contact, including sexual contact, or fomites spreads human papillomavirus warts on the skin. Parvovirus B19 instead spreads by droplet infection, the same route as the adenoviruses.
Contaminated food

Ingestion of contaminated food or water is a route listed for the polyomaviruses. Parvovirus B19 spreads by droplet infection, a route it shares with the adenoviruses and their respiratory secretions.

set1.q: Why was variolation replaced by vaccination?
opts: It caused facial tumor growths

Tumor-like growths on the face are the atypical form of molluscum contagiosum in acquired immunodeficiency syndrome. The problem with variolation was that variolated people spread collateral cases of smallpox.
It infected pet prairie dogs

Prairie dogs were infected with mpox from African rodents housed in the same animal vendor facility, not by variolation. Variolation was abandoned because the smallpox cases spread by variolated people outweighed the benefits.
It ended herd immunity to pox

Loss of herd immunity is linked to the end of smallpox vaccination and is thought to explain re-emerging cowpox cases. Variolation gave way to vaccination because variolated people spread collateral smallpox cases.
It seeded new smallpox cases

Correct. Variolation did not always work and sometimes failed to protect during an epidemic, and the collateral smallpox cases spread by variolated people began to outweigh its benefits. Vaccination was less harmful, and variolation was made illegal in some countries.

set1.q: How do adenoviruses mainly spread from person to person?
opts: Contact with saliva alone
Contact with saliva is the route for human herpesviruses 6 and 7 (roseola). Adenoviruses spread through respiratory and ocular secretions as droplets, which explains their eye infections.
Respiratory and ocular secretions

Correct. Adenoviruses spread by respiratory and ocular secretions (droplet infection), which fits where they infect: respiratory epithelium and the conjunctiva, causing colds, pharyngitis and conjunctivitis.
Blood and sexual contact
Blood, serum and sexual contact transmit hepatitis B virus, a risk for health care workers. Adenoviruses spread by respiratory and ocular secretions, matching their colds and conjunctivitis.
Direct skin contact and fomites
Direct contact or contaminated fomites is how human papillomavirus spreads its warts. Adenoviruses travel in respiratory and ocular secretions, infecting respiratory epithelium and the conjunctiva.

set1.q: Which description fits a herpesvirus virion and its deoxyribonucleic acid genome?
opts: Nonenveloped, single-stranded

A nonenveloped virus with single-stranded deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) and a small diameter and genome is a parvovirus, such as B19. Herpesviruses are enveloped and carry double-stranded deoxyribonucleic acid inside an icosahedral capsid.
Nonenveloped, circular, double-stranded

Small, nonenveloped viruses with circular double-stranded deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) are the papilloma and polyoma viruses. A herpesvirus has an envelope with glycoprotein spikes around its icosahedral capsid; the envelope is the tell.
Enveloped, partly single-stranded

An enveloped virus whose unusual genome holds both double- and single-stranded deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) is a hepadnavirus, hepatitis B. Herpesvirus deoxyribonucleic acid is fully double-stranded, inside a large icosahedral capsid under its envelope.
Enveloped, icosahedral, double-stranded

Correct. Herpesviruses are large, enveloped, icosahedral viruses with double-stranded deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA). The virion has glycoprotein spikes on its envelope, a tegument layer beneath it, and a capsid holding the deoxyribonucleic acid core.

set1.q: Most cytomegalovirus infections are asymptomatic. Which group develops a more virulent form of the disease?
opts: Wrestlers and rugby players
Athletes in wrestling, basketball or rugby are prone to herpes gladiatorum, a herpes simplex skin infection. Severe cytomegalovirus disease strikes fetuses, newborns and immunodeficient adults.
Healthy older adults

Older patients are more likely to get shingles from varicella zoster virus. Healthy age alone does not make cytomegalovirus virulent; the three groups are fetuses, newborns and immunodeficient adults.
Immunodeficient adults

Correct. Three groups develop a more virulent cytomegalovirus disease: fetuses, newborns and immunodeficient adults. In acquired immunodeficiency syndrome it causes retinitis and disseminated disease, and most transplant patients get pneumonitis or hepatitis; treatment is reserved for the immunocompromised.
College-age young adults

The college-age population in industrialized countries is the group vulnerable to infectious mononucleosis from Epstein-Barr virus. The virulent cytomegalovirus groups are fetuses, newborns and immunodeficient adults.

set1.q: Poxviruses show specificity for the cytoplasm of which cells, which leads to their pustules?
opts: Epidermal cells

Correct. Poxviruses have a specificity for the cytoplasm of epidermal cells and subcutaneous connective tissue. That is what produces their eruptive skin pustules, the pocks or pox that leave scars, and it can also stimulate tumor formation.
Trigeminal ganglion cells

The trigeminal ganglion is where herpes simplex virus type 1 lies latent after entering the fifth cranial nerve, not a target of poxviruses. Poxviruses home to the cytoplasm of epidermal cells and subcutaneous connective tissue, which is why they make skin pustules.
B lymphocytes

B cells are where Epstein-Barr virus stays dormant, and Burkitt lymphoma is a B-cell malignancy linked to it. Poxviruses instead have specificity for the cytoplasm of epidermal cells and subcutaneous connective tissue, giving pocks on the skin.
Liver cells

Liver cells are the target of hepatitis B virus, which raises the risk of hepatocellular carcinoma. Poxviruses are skin viruses: their specificity for the cytoplasm of epidermal cells and subcutaneous connective tissue produces the eruptive pustules called pocks.

set1.io: 2 — Compare and contrast the characteristics of a lytic viral infection versus a persistent chronic or persistent latent infection.
set1.q: Which type of infection does hepatitis B virus establish, with virus detectable in tissue and multiplying slowly?
opts: Acute lytic
Acute infections take a rapid lytic course, as in colds and flu, and do not persist for years. Hepatitis B virus persists, detectable and slowly multiplying: a chronic infection.
Lysogenic
Lysogenic is a phage cycle in bacteria, the prophage replicated with the host chromosome. In human viral infection, hepatitis B virus is the example of a persistent chronic infection.
Persistent chronic

Correct. Chronic infections keep the virus detectable in tissue samples, multiplying at a slow rate, with mild or absent symptoms; hepatitis B virus and human immunodeficiency virus are the examples. Chronic infection may involve integration of viral genetic material into the host chromosome.
Persistent latent
Latent infections, the herpesviruses' pattern, go dormant after a lytic cycle and are generally not detectable. Hepatitis B virus stays detectable and multiplies slowly, a chronic infection.

set1.q: An enveloped animal virus attaches to its host cell. Which viral structure binds the cell receptors?
opts: Its matrix

The matrix is a layer inside the envelope, around the capsid, not on the surface. Surface spikes are what bind the cell receptors during adsorption. To tell them apart: only the spikes project from the envelope surface, where receptors sit.
Its spikes

Correct. In adsorption the virus attaches to its host cell by specific binding of its spikes to cell receptors. This receptor fit is also why viruses are limited to a particular host or cell type. To tell them apart: tail fibers are phage parts; spikes are animal virus parts.
Its tail fibers
Tail fibers are part of a bacteriophage, which adsorbs to bacteria and injects its genome. An enveloped animal virus attaches by specific binding of its envelope spikes to cell receptors.
Its nucleic acid

The nucleic acid lies inside the capsid and is freed only after uncoating, inside the cell. Attachment uses the spikes on the envelope, which bind specific cell receptors. To tell them apart: attachment is on the outside.

set1.q: A pregnant woman with genital herpes has an active outbreak when labor begins. Which delivery is advised to protect the infant?
opts: Vaginal delivery, then infant screening
Screening is done on the pregnant woman, before birth, not as a substitute for a safe delivery. With an active outbreak at birth, the infant is protected by delivery by cesarean section.
Delivery by cesarean section

Correct. Herpes of the newborn is prevented by screening pregnant women and by delivery by cesarean section if there is an outbreak at the time of birth, because the infant is otherwise contaminated by the mother during birth.
Vaginal delivery after vaccination
There is no herpes simplex vaccine: only candidate vaccines in trials and ongoing research. With an outbreak at the time of birth, the infant is protected by delivery by cesarean section.
Vaginal delivery once lesions crust

A cold sore crusts over in a few days and heals, but genital herpes can spread even without visible lesions, and labor will not wait. An outbreak at the time of birth calls for delivery by cesarean section.

set1.io: 3 — Differentiate between oncogenic and teratogenic viruses.
set1.q: Nine human papillomavirus types increase the risk of cancer in which body system?
opts: Reproductive system

Correct. Nine human papillomavirus types increase the risk of developing reproductive system cancer; papillomaviruses are linked to cervical and penile cancer. Women are screened by Pap smear for abnormal cervical cells.
Hepatic system
Liver cancer, hepatocellular carcinoma, is the cancer risk of chronic hepatitis B virus infection. The human papillomavirus types raise the risk of reproductive cancers, cervical and penile.
Lymphatic system
Lymphatic cancer such as Burkitt lymphoma is tied to Epstein-Barr virus. Human papillomavirus types raise the risk of reproductive system cancers, such as cervical and penile cancer.
Nervous system

The nervous system disease among these deoxyribonucleic acid viruses is progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy from JC polyomavirus, a demyelinating infection, not a cancer. Human papillomavirus raises reproductive cancer risk.

set1.q: Patients with Crohn disease or ulcerative colitis show a shift in gut virome composition. What does this shift establish?
opts: Phages protect the bowel
No protective role is stated; phages may even compromise colonization of normal flora. The virome shift in inflammatory bowel disease is an association whose cause and effect is unproven.
A link, cause not proven

Correct. Some studies show a shift in virome composition in inflammatory bowel disease, Crohn disease or ulcerative colitis, but this may or may not be a cause-and-effect relationship. It is an observed association, not proof that phages cause the disease.
Phages cause the disease
No cause has been shown: the virome shift may or may not be a cause-and-effect relationship. Reading it as proof that phages cause inflammatory bowel disease goes beyond what the studies show.
The disease destroys phages
The reverse direction is not shown either; the studies record only a change in virome composition, which may or may not be cause and effect. It is an association, cause not proven.

set1.q: After initial infection through the tonsils or gastrointestinal tract, where does JC polyomavirus remain latent?
opts: Gut and kidney tubular cells

Correct. After initial infection via the tonsils or gastrointestinal tract, JC virus is latent in the gastrointestinal tract and the tubular epithelial cells of the kidneys, shedding virus in urine. It can cross the blood-brain barrier in immunosuppressed patients.
The trigeminal ganglion
The trigeminal ganglion is where herpes simplex virus type 1 stays latent after entering the fifth cranial nerve. JC polyomavirus stays latent in the gastrointestinal tract and kidney tubular cells.
Liver cells

Liver cells are where hepatitis B virus multiplies exclusively, seeding the blood in a chronic infection. JC polyomavirus is latent in the gastrointestinal tract and the tubular epithelium of the kidneys.
Lymphoid tissue
Lymphoid tissue, along with respiratory and intestinal epithelia and conjunctiva, is what adenoviruses infect. JC polyomavirus lies latent in the gastrointestinal tract and kidney tubular cells.

set1.io: 4 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of DNA viruses of medical importance.
set1.q: A bacteriophage has a head joined to a tail with a sheath and tail fibers. Which capsid type is this?
opts: Enveloped

An envelope is not a capsid shape at all: it is a membrane layer some animal viruses gain during budding, outside the capsid. Capsids are helical, icosahedral or complex, and the tailed phage is the complex one.
Complex

Correct. Viral capsids come in three shapes: helical, icosahedral and complex, and the complex shape is the phage type. The head-and-tail build, with sheath, plug and tail fibers below a capsid head, is what makes a phage capsid complex rather than a simple rod or a many-sided solid.
Helical

A helical capsid is a rod of capsid units wound around the nucleic acid, the nucleocapsid drawn as a single spiral column. A phage adds a tail, sheath and tail fibers to its head, which is the complex type.
Icosahedral

An icosahedral capsid is the many-sided solid seen in naked and enveloped animal viruses such as the papovavirus. The phage's head sits on a tail with sheath and fibers, so the whole capsid is complex.

set1.q: Of the three principal viruses that cause hepatitis, which one is a deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) virus?
opts: Hepatitis A virus

Hepatitis A virus is one of the three principal hepatitis viruses, but it is a ribonucleic acid (RNA) virus. The deoxyribonucleic acid virus of the three is hepatitis B virus, an enveloped hepadnavirus.
Hepatitis C virus

Hepatitis C virus is the third principal hepatitis virus and, like hepatitis A, a ribonucleic acid (RNA) virus. Only hepatitis B virus carries deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA), with its unusual partly double-stranded, partly single-stranded genome.
Hepatitis D virus

Hepatitis D, the delta agent, is a circular ribonucleic acid (RNA) virus and not one of the three principal hepatitis viruses; it is known for co-infecting with hepatitis B virus and making severe disease worse. The deoxyribonucleic acid virus is hepatitis B.
Hepatitis B virus

Correct. Hepatitis B virus is the deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) virus among the three principal hepatitis viruses; hepatitis A and hepatitis C viruses are ribonucleic acid (RNA) viruses. It belongs to the hepadnaviruses, enveloped deoxyribonucleic acid viruses with a tropism for the liver.

set1.io: 3 — Differentiate between oncogenic and teratogenic viruses.
set1.q: Besides a family history, which risk factor is listed for nasopharyngeal carcinoma, an Epstein-Barr virus-associated tumor?
opts: Eating salt-cured foods

Correct. Nasopharyngeal carcinoma is a malignancy of epithelial cells occurring in adults, older Chinese and African men, those with a family history and those who eat salt-cured foods. It presents with a lump in the neck, hearing loss and a blocked nasal passage.
Playing contact sports
Contact sports such as wrestling, basketball and rugby spread herpes gladiatorum, a herpes simplex skin infection. Nasopharyngeal carcinoma risk comes with family history and eating salt-cured foods.
Handling sheep or goats

Handling sheep or goats transmits orf virus, a parapoxvirus that causes sores. The listed risk factors for nasopharyngeal carcinoma are older age in certain groups, family history and salt-cured foods.
Receiving a kidney transplant

A renal transplant with immunosuppressive drugs is the setting for BK polyomavirus disease. Nasopharyngeal carcinoma, linked to Epstein-Barr virus, is tied to family history and eating salt-cured foods.

set1.io: 2 — Compare and contrast the characteristics of a lytic viral infection versus a persistent chronic or persistent latent infection.
set1.q: During latency, how does a herpesvirus infection differ from a persistent chronic infection?
opts: The virus multiplies slowly in tissue

Slow, ongoing multiplication that can be detected in tissue samples is the chronic infection, as with human immunodeficiency virus and hepatitis B virus. A latent herpesvirus is dormant and generally undetectable until it reactivates.
The host cell is destroyed quickly

Rapid destruction of the host cell is a lytic cycle, the course of acute agents such as colds and flu. A latent herpesvirus leaves the cell alive, holding its deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) as an episome until a trigger reactivates it.
Its genes replicate as a prophage

A prophage is phage deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) integrated into a bacterial chromosome and copied with it, the lysogenic cycle. A latent herpesvirus keeps its deoxyribonucleic acid as an episome in the nucleus, not integrated, and is generally not detectable.
The virus is generally not detectable

Correct. In a latent infection, after a lytic cycle, the herpesvirus enters a dormant phase: it is generally not detectable and causes no symptoms, yet it can reactivate later. In a chronic infection the virus stays detectable in tissue samples, multiplying slowly.

set1.io: 3 — Differentiate between oncogenic and teratogenic viruses.
set1.q: Epstein-Barr virus is oncogenic. Which cancer is it linked with?
opts: Kaposi sarcoma

Kaposi sarcoma is the tumor of human herpesvirus 8, a different herpesvirus. Epstein-Barr virus is the one linked with Burkitt lymphoma. To tell them apart: Kaposi sarcoma shows as small painless discolored skin lumps, often in acquired immunodeficiency syndrome, not as a lymphoma.
Hepatic carcinoma

Hepatic carcinoma is linked with persistent hepatitis B virus, a hepadnavirus, not a herpesvirus. Epstein-Barr virus is paired with Burkitt lymphoma. To tell them apart: the liver cancer belongs to hepatitis B virus, the lymphoma to Epstein-Barr virus.
Cervical cancer
Cervical and penile cancer are linked with the papillomaviruses, nonenveloped double-stranded viruses. Epstein-Barr virus, an enveloped herpesvirus, is linked with Burkitt lymphoma.
Burkitt lymphoma

Correct. Among persistent oncogenic viruses, Epstein-Barr virus is linked with Burkitt lymphoma. The other pairings are human herpesvirus 8 with Kaposi sarcoma, hepatitis B virus with hepatic carcinoma, and papillomaviruses with cervical and penile cancer.

set1.q: What is the natural host range of varicella zoster virus?
opts: Humans and rodents
Rodents are the primary reservoirs of cowpox, which humans catch rarely, often by handling cats that interacted with rodents. Varicella zoster virus has humans as its only natural host.
Humans and sheep
Sheep and goats carry orf virus, a parapoxvirus that humans catch by feeding, shearing or bites. Varicella zoster virus has no animal host: humans are its only natural host.
Humans and cattle
Cowpox is found in cows as well as rodents, cats and zoo animals. Varicella zoster virus infects only humans naturally, spreading by respiratory droplets and fluid from active lesions.
Humans only

Correct. Varicella zoster virus, the cause of chickenpox and shingles, has humans as its only natural host. It passes from person to person by respiratory droplets and by contact with fluid from active skin lesions.

set1.q: Why is a given virus limited to a particular host or cell type?
opts: Presence of an envelope

An envelope comes from budding and helps evade the immune system; it is a classification feature, not the host limit. Host and cell range depend on receptor compatibility. To tell them apart: the fit is at the receptor.
Mode of transmission
Transmission decides how a virus reaches a person, such as droplets or direct contact, not which cells it can infect. Host and cell type are set by compatibility of receptors and genetic material.
Receptor compatibility

Correct. Viruses are limited to a particular host or cell type by compatibility of receptors and genetic material. At adsorption the virus attaches by specific binding of its spikes to the cell receptors, so cells without a matching receptor are not infected.
Genome size

Genome size is not what limits the host; the limit is compatibility of receptors and genetic material, with spikes binding specific cell receptors at adsorption. To tell them apart: specificity is a lock-and-key fit at the cell surface, not a matter of size.

set2.io: 1 — Recall the steps of DNA virus replication.
set2.q: Which process carries random pieces of host DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) from one bacterium to other bacteria?
opts: Specialized transduction
Specialized transduction belongs to the lysogenic cycle, and in it all cells carry the same DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) from the host, not random pieces. Random pieces mark generalized transduction.
Lysogenic conversion

Lysogenic conversion is one of the phage-bacterium interactions in the gut, a bacterium changed by its prophage, such as gaining a new trait. Random host pieces moved to other bacteria are generalized transduction.
Prophage induction

Prophage induction is the shock that releases a prophage from the host chromosome to start a lytic cycle. Carrying random pieces of host DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) to other bacteria is generalized transduction.
Generalized transduction

Correct. Generalized transduction, listed with the lytic cycle, means random pieces of the host DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) may be transmitted to other bacteria. In specialized transduction, from the lysogenic cycle, all cells carry the same DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) from the host.

set2.io: 5 — Compare and contrast the mode of transmission, clinical manifestations, and availability of a vaccine for DNA viruses of medical importance.
set2.q: Besides blood and blood products, by which other route is hepatitis B virus transmitted?
opts: Contact with saliva

Contact with saliva spreads human herpesviruses 6 and 7 (roseola) and Epstein-Barr virus. Hepatitis B virus is a blood-borne virus that is also sexually transmitted, which is why it is a risk for health care workers.
Sexual contact

Correct. Minute amounts of blood or blood products transmit hepatitis B virus, and it is also sexually transmitted, which is why it has a high incidence in the same population as human immunodeficiency virus. It enters through a break in the skin or mucous membrane or by injection.
Respiratory droplets

Droplet infection is how adenoviruses and parvovirus B19 spread, through respiratory secretions. Hepatitis B virus is carried in blood and serum and is also sexually transmitted, entering through skin or mucous membrane breaks.
Contaminated food or water

Ingestion of contaminated food or water is a listed route for the polyomaviruses, alongside exposure to body fluids. Hepatitis B virus needs blood or serum contact, or sexual contact, to reach the bloodstream and liver.

set2.q: Which is a route by which smallpox spreads?

Contact with infected pet prairie dogs spread mpox in a United States outbreak. Smallpox has no animal source: it requires a human host and spreads by inhaled airborne saliva and contact with pustule material or fomites.
Inhaled airborne saliva

Correct. Smallpox spreads from person to person by inhalation of airborne saliva, by contact with material from pustules or scabs, and by fomites contaminated with that material. Variola requires a human host, so animals play no part.
Shearing infected sheep

Shearing, feeding and bites from sheep and goats pass orf virus, a parapox virus, to people who handle the animals. Variola has no animal host; smallpox passes from person to person, by inhaled saliva, contact with pustule material, or fomites.
A rodent-hunting pet cat

Handling a cat that interacted with rodents is how people catch cowpox, usually on the hands. Smallpox needs a human host and spreads person to person through airborne saliva, contact with pustules or scabs, and fomites.

set2.io: 2 — Compare and contrast the characteristics of a lytic viral infection versus a persistent chronic or persistent latent infection.
set2.q: Herpesviruses typically establish which kind of infection?
opts: Persistent latent

Correct. Herpesviruses are the example of latent infection: after a lytic cycle the virus enters a dormant phase, generally not detectable and without symptoms, and can reactivate to cause recurrent infections. Its DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) stays in the nucleus without integrating.
Persistent chronic
Chronic infection, detectable and slowly multiplying, is the pattern of human immunodeficiency virus and hepatitis B virus. Herpesviruses go dormant and reactivate: latent infection.
Acute only

Acute infections run a rapid lytic course and end, like colds and flu. Herpesviruses begin with a lytic cycle but then persist dormant and can reactivate, a latent infection. To tell them apart: herpes recurs.
Teratogenic
Teratogenic describes viruses that cross the placenta and cause developmental defects, such as rubella and cytomegalovirus; it is not an infection course. Herpesviruses establish latent infection.

set2.io: 3 — Differentiate between oncogenic and teratogenic viruses.
set2.q: Besides rubella, which virus is teratogenic, able to cross the placenta and cause permanent defects?
opts: Hepatitis B virus
Hepatitis B virus is a chronic, oncogenic virus linked with hepatic carcinoma. Crossing the placenta to cause permanent defects is the teratogenic trait of rubella and cytomegalovirus.
Human herpesvirus 8

Human herpesvirus 8 is oncogenic, linked with Kaposi sarcoma. The teratogenic viruses named are rubella and cytomegalovirus. To tell them apart: the tumor it causes makes it oncogenic; only rubella and cytomegalovirus are named as crossing the placenta to cause defects.
Cytomegalovirus

Correct. Several viruses cross the placenta, causing developmental disturbances and permanent defects; rubella and cytomegalovirus are the teratogenic examples. Fetuses infected with cytomegalovirus may show microcephaly, and survivors can have neurological, hearing and visual problems.
Epstein-Barr virus

Epstein-Barr virus is oncogenic, linked with Burkitt lymphoma, not teratogenic. The teratogenic pair is rubella and cytomegalovirus. To tell them apart: a cancer link makes a virus oncogenic; a placental route to fetal defects makes it teratogenic.

set2.q: A blood smear from a patient with an Epstein-Barr virus infection shows the cell indicated by the arrows. What is it?
opts: A giant multinucleated cell
Giant multinucleated cells come from scrapings at the base of herpes simplex lesions and hold many nuclei. The pictured blood cell has one nucleus and is a large atypical lymphocyte.
A cell with an owl's-eye inclusion
An owl's eye inclusion, a large inclusion inside the nucleus of an enlarged cell, is the cytomegalovirus change. The pictured blood cell shows no such inclusion; it is a large atypical lymphocyte.
A large atypical lymphocyte

Correct. Epstein-Barr virus infection gives lymphocytosis with large atypical lymphocytes. Compared with a normal small, round lymphocyte, the infected cell is much larger, with an irregular nucleus and abundant pale cytoplasm pressed between the red blood cells.
A normal small lymphocyte

A normal lymphocyte is small and round, mostly nucleus, about the size of the nearby red blood cells. The pictured cell is far larger with abundant cytoplasm: the large atypical lymphocyte of Epstein-Barr virus.

set2.q: Which feature separates a persistent chronic infection from a persistent latent one?
opts: Severe ongoing symptoms
Chronic infection has mild or absent symptoms, and latent infection has none while dormant, so severity does not separate them. Chronic virus is detectable in tissue; latent virus generally is not.
Virus detectable in tissue

Correct. In chronic infection the virus is detectable in tissue samples, multiplying at a slow rate. In latent infection the virus enters a dormant phase after a lytic cycle and is generally not detectable, until it reactivates.
Infection lasting for years
Both kinds are persistent infections lasting many years or a lifetime, so duration does not separate them. Detectability does: chronic virus is detectable in tissue, latent virus generally is not.
Reactivation with recurrences
Reactivation causing recurrent infection is the mark of latent infection, as with the herpesviruses, not chronic. Chronic infection is set apart by virus detectable in tissue, multiplying slowly.

opts: Plantar warts
Plantar warts are deep and painful and sit on the soles of the feet. These growths are on the fingers, painless and raised: common seed warts from human papillomavirus.
Genital warts
Genital warts range from tiny flat bumps to branching cauliflower-like masses on the genitals. Raised, rough, painless growths on the fingers are common seed warts.
Molluscum contagiosum lesions
Molluscum contagiosum gives small, smooth, waxy lesions, often in the genital area and on the thighs. The growths shown are rough and elevated on the fingers, the picture of common seed warts.
Common seed warts

Correct. Common seed warts are painless, elevated, rough growths on the fingers and similar sites, as on the hand shown. They are papillomas caused by human papillomavirus, spread by direct contact or fomites; most regress over time.

set2.q: In the replication of a DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) animal virus, which step comes right after entry and uncoating?
opts: Maturation of virions
Maturation is the sixth step, after capsid proteins are made, just before release. Directly after uncoating, part of the viral DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) is transcribed for early proteins.
Release by budding
Release of virions by budding is the last step of the seven. Directly after entry and uncoating, a portion of the viral DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) is transcribed for early proteins.
Transcription for early proteins

Correct. After the virion enters and its DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) is uncoated, a portion of the viral DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) is transcribed, producing messenger RNA (ribonucleic acid) that encodes early viral proteins. Biosynthesis, late translation of capsid proteins, maturation and release follow.
Late translation of capsids

Late translation, when capsid proteins are synthesized, comes after early transcription and biosynthesis of viral DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid). The step straight after uncoating is transcription for early proteins.

A Papanicolaou (Pap) smear is a stained specimen used to diagnose herpes infection and to screen for abnormal cervical cells; it does not prevent mat herpes. Mat herpes is prevented by showering after practice and not sharing personal items.
Showering right after practice

Correct. These are herpes gladiatorum, mat herpes, a skin infection common in wrestling, basketball and rugby players. It may be prevented by showering immediately after practice or games and by not sharing razors, deodorants or towels.
A live attenuated vaccine
A live attenuated vaccine exists for chickenpox and shingles, from varicella zoster virus. Mat herpes is prevented by showering promptly and not sharing razors, deodorants or towels.
Sharing towels only with teammates

Sharing towels, razors or deodorants is exactly what should be avoided, since herpes simplex spreads by direct exposure to secretions from lesions. Showering right after practice and keeping personal items personal are the listed measures.

set2.q: After an animal virus is engulfed, what drives the uncoating that frees its genetic material?
opts: Viral lysozyme

Viral lysozyme is the phage's tool, used with the tail pin to breach the bacterial wall and later to burst it at release. Animal virus uncoating depends on the pH of the cytoplasm against the extracellular fluid.
A shock to the cell

A shock of some kind is what induces a prophage to leave the bacterial chromosome in the lysogenic cycle. Animal virus uncoating is driven by a pH difference between cytoplasm and extracellular fluid.
Receptor binding
Binding of the virus's spikes to cell receptors is adsorption, the first step, before engulfment. Uncoating inside the cell is driven by the pH of the cytoplasm against the extracellular fluid.
A difference in pH

Correct. Animal viruses need uncoating to release their genetic material, and the trigger is the pH of the cytoplasm compared with the extracellular fluid. Phages need no uncoating because only their DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) is injected.

set2.q: Why did smallpox tend to be present in densely populated areas?
opts: It requires a human host

Correct. Variola virus requires a human host, so smallpox persisted where people were crowded together, in densely populated areas, with epidemics recurring at regular intervals. It spreads from person to person by inhaled airborne saliva, direct contact and fomites.
Rodents are its main reservoir

Rodents seem to be the primary reservoir of cowpox, which reaches people through cats that interact with rodents. Variola has no animal reservoir: it requires a human host, which is why smallpox clustered in densely populated areas.
It spreads by handling sheep

Handling sheep and goats, by feeding, shearing or bites, is how people catch orf virus, a parapox virus of ruminant animals. Smallpox needs a human host and spreads from person to person, so crowded populations sustained it.
Pet prairie dogs carry it

Pet prairie dogs carried mpox in a United States outbreak, after picking it up from rodents imported from Africa. Variola has no animal host at all; it requires humans, so it lingered in densely populated areas.

Host cell type is not among the features used to group animal viruses. Animal viruses are grouped by nucleic acid, capsid and whether an envelope is present.
Their mode of spread
Mode of transmission is listed per virus (droplets, direct contact, blood) but is not how the families are built. The grouping uses nucleic acid, capsid and presence or absence of an envelope.
Their tail structure

A tail is a feature of the complex capsid of bacteriophages, viruses of bacteria, not an animal virus grouping feature. Animal viruses are grouped by nucleic acid, capsid and presence or absence of an envelope.
Presence of an envelope

Correct. Animal viruses are categorized according to nucleic acid, capsid, and presence or absence of an envelope. That is why the human DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) virus groups split first into enveloped and nonenveloped viruses, then by double-stranded or single-stranded genome.

Correct. Scrapings from the base of herpes simplex lesions show giant multinucleated cells and inclusion bodies. In this stained Papanicolaou (Pap) specimen, the large central cell holds a long chain of many nuclei, surrounded by normal cells.
A large atypical lymphocyte

A large atypical lymphocyte, with one big nucleus and abundant cytoplasm, is seen in the blood count in Epstein-Barr virus infection. The pictured cell came from a vesicle base and holds many nuclei: a giant multinucleated cell.
A cell with one owl's-eye nucleus

Molluscum contagiosum virus

Monkeypox virus

Correct. Fever, chills and swollen lymph nodes, then a pustular rash spreading over the body, after contact with an infected animal, point to monkeypox virus (mpox). Humans are susceptible to it and to cowpox among the animal poxviruses, and mpox gives skin pocks, fever and swollen lymph nodes.

set2.q: Erythema infectiosum is the fifth rash disease of childhood. Which is one of the other four?
opts: Infantile gastroenteritis
Infantile gastroenteritis is an adenovirus disease of the intestinal epithelium, without a defining rash. The other four childhood rash diseases are chickenpox, measles, rubella and roseola.
Roseola

Correct. Erythema infectiosum (fifth disease, from parvovirus B19) is the fifth rash disease of childhood; the other four are chickenpox, measles, rubella and roseola. Roseola, from human herpesviruses 6 and 7, is an acute febrile disease followed by rash.
Molluscum contagiosum

Molluscum contagiosum is a poxvirus skin infection with small, smooth, waxy lesions, often in the genital area and on the thighs, not one of the childhood rash diseases. Those are chickenpox, measles, rubella and roseola.
Infectious mononucleosis

set2.q: Besides eruptive skin pustules, what else can the poxviruses' specificity for epidermal cells and subcutaneous connective tissue stimulate?

Crossing the placenta to cause developmental disturbances and permanent defects is what teratogenic viruses do, such as rubella and cytomegalovirus. The poxviruses' specificity for epidermal cells and subcutaneous connective tissue instead gives pustules or tumor formation.
Myelin destruction

Destruction of the cells that make myelin is the hallmark of progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy from JC polyomavirus. Poxviruses act on the skin: their tissue specificity gives pustules or can stimulate tumor formation.
Dermatomal vesicles

Vesicles along a dermatome are shingles, the reactivation of latent varicella zoster virus along a nerve pathway. Poxviruses cause scarring pustules, the pocks, and their specificity for epidermal cells and subcutaneous connective tissue can also stimulate tumor formation.
Tumor formation

Correct. The specificity of poxviruses for the cytoplasm of epidermal cells and subcutaneous connective tissue leads to the pustules, or it can stimulate tumor formation. Routine childhood clinics
Smallpox vaccine is no longer routinely given, so childhood clinics do not hold it. Vaccines and treatments for an emergency are kept in the Strategic National Stockpile.
The Strategic National Stockpile

Correct. Smallpox vaccines and treatments are kept in the Strategic National Stockpile, a store of medical supplies for a public health emergency. It holds three smallpox vaccines, including ACAM2000 and JYNNEOS, because smallpox is a potential bioterrorism weapon.
The two smallpox research labs
Only two laboratories work with smallpox itself, one in Atlanta and one in Russia. The vaccines and treatments kept ready for an emergency sit in the Strategic National Stockpile, not in those labs.

set2.q: Why may phage therapy trials give relatively unpredictable results?
opts: Phages infecting human cells

The host cells of bacteriophages are bacterial cells, though phages may still affect human health. The unpredictability comes from complex phage-bacterium relationships, such as strain specificity and resistance.
Phages lacking strain specificity

This reverses the fact: phages are bacterial strain specific. That specificity, along with protected bacteria and shifting interactions, is part of the complex relationships that make therapy trials unpredictable.
Phages lacking nucleic acid

Every virus contains genetic material, DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) or RNA (ribonucleic acid), and phage nucleic acids may even stimulate an immune response. Trial unpredictability stems from complex phage-bacteria relationships.
Complex phage-bacteria relationships

Correct. Phages are bacterial strain specific, the gut environment protects some bacteria, interactions can be antagonistic or mutualistic and may change over time through evolution. These complex relationships may explain the relative unpredictability of phage therapy trials.

set2.q: Which of these can transmit cytomegalovirus?

Breast milk
Correct. Cytomegalovirus is transmitted in saliva, respiratory mucus, breast milk, urine, semen, cervical secretions, blood and tears, and in tissues such as transplants.
Handling sheep or goats

Handling sheep or goats, by feeding, shearing or bites, transmits orf virus, a parapoxvirus. Cytomegalovirus is a human virus spread in body fluids such as saliva, breast milk, urine and semen, and in transplanted tissue.
Handling a rodent-hunting cat

Handling cats that interacted with rodents passes cowpox to humans, usually on the hands. Cytomegalovirus spreads through body fluids, including breast milk, saliva and urine, and through transplants.

set2.q: A farmer has the ulcerated lesion shown on the back of the hand after feeding and shearing his sheep. In the animals, what is this virus's disease called?
opts: Contagious ecthyma

Correct. A hand lesion after feeding and shearing sheep is orf, a parapox virus of sheep and goats. In the animals it causes sores on the mouth, called sore mouth, scabby mouth or contagious ecthyma. It is more serious in the immunocompromised.
Molluscum contagiosum

Molluscum contagiosum is a human poxvirus disease spread by direct contact and fomites, with small, smooth, waxy lesions; it is not a disease of sheep. Orf virus in sheep and goats causes contagious ecthyma, also called sore mouth or scabby mouth.
Variola minor

Variola minor is the less virulent form of smallpox, a virus that requires a human host and has no animal form. The sheep and goat disease spread by feeding and shearing is orf, called contagious ecthyma in the animals.
Rabbitpox

Rabbitpox is the poxvirus of rabbits, one of many mammalian poxviruses. The sheep and goat disease spread by feeding and shearing is orf, called sore mouth, scabby mouth or contagious ecthyma in the animals.

set2.io: 5 — Compare and contrast the mode of transmission, clinical manifestations, and availability of a vaccine for DNA viruses of medical importance.
set2.q: From what is the main hepatitis B vaccine derived?
opts: Adenovirus types 4 and 7
A vaccine against adenovirus types 4 and 7 is given to some military personnel in training. Hepatitis B vaccine is a single antigen, the surface antigen, cloned in yeast, not a mix of virus types.
An adeno-associated virus vector

Adeno-associated virus is used as a vector for human gene therapy, approved to treat lipoprotein lipase deficiency, not as a hepatitis vaccine. The hepatitis B vaccine is built from surface antigen cloned in yeast.
Surface antigen cloned in yeast

Correct. Hepatitis B vaccines are derived from surface antigen from cloned yeast, given with boosters. Vaccination is the primary prevention for high-risk people and is encouraged for all newborns and infants. A second vaccine, made from antigen purified from carrier blood, is mainly for people with yeast allergies.
Live vaccinia virus

Live vaccinia virus is the smallpox vaccine (ACAM2000 is one), also made available to prevent mpox. Hepatitis B vaccination uses no live virus: the main vaccine is surface antigen produced from cloned yeast.

set2.io: 4 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of DNA viruses of medical importance.
set2.q: Which description fits the adenovirus virion and genome?
opts: Nonenveloped; double-stranded

Correct. Adenoviruses are nonenveloped, double-stranded deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) viruses that cause acute infections. They infect lymphoid tissue, respiratory and intestinal epithelia and the conjunctiva, and spread by respiratory and ocular secretions.
Enveloped; partly single-stranded

An envelope with a partly double-, partly single-stranded genome describes hepatitis B virus, a hepadnavirus. Adenoviruses have no envelope and carry fully double-stranded deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA).
Nonenveloped; single-stranded

Nonenveloped with single-stranded deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) is the parvovirus pattern, small viruses such as parvovirus B19. Adenoviruses share the lack of an envelope but their genome is double-stranded.
Enveloped; double-stranded

Adenoviruses are listed among the nonenveloped deoxyribonucleic acid viruses, alongside the polyoma, papilloma and parvo viruses. Their genome is double-stranded deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) inside a bare capsid, with no envelope.

set2.io: 3 — Differentiate between oncogenic and teratogenic viruses.
set2.q: Human herpesvirus 7 is closely related to human herpesvirus 6. How are these viruses tied to cancers such as Hodgkin lymphoma?
opts: By association, not causation

Correct. There is an association, not causation, between human herpesvirus 6 and Hodgkin lymphoma, oral carcinoma and certain T-cell leukemias. Human herpesvirus 7 is closely related, causes similar diseases such as roseola, and is also associated with cancers.
As their proven direct cause

Causation is exactly what is not shown: the link between human herpesvirus 6 and these cancers is an association, not causation. Oncogenic links stated as such include Epstein-Barr virus with Burkitt lymphoma.
By crossing the placenta
Crossing the placenta to cause developmental defects is what teratogenic viruses, rubella and cytomegalovirus, do. Human herpesviruses 6 and 7 have only an association, not causation, with cancers.
They have no link to cancer

A link is described: human herpesvirus 6 is associated with Hodgkin lymphoma, oral carcinoma and certain T-cell leukemias, and human herpesvirus 7 is also associated with cancers. The link is association, not causation.

set2.io: 4 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of DNA viruses of medical importance.
set2.q: Which property lets JC polyomavirus cause progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy in immunosuppressed patients?
opts: It can cross the blood-brain barrier

Correct. JC virus can cross the blood-brain barrier, and in immunosuppressed patients it destroys the cells that produce myelin, causing progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy, an uncommon, often fatal infection.
It enters the fifth cranial nerve
Entering the fifth cranial nerve is how herpes simplex virus type 1 reaches the trigeminal ganglion. JC virus reaches the brain by crossing the blood-brain barrier.
It is a defective helper virus

A defective virus that cannot replicate without a helper is adeno-associated virus, which needs adenovirus. JC virus replicates on its own and causes brain disease by crossing the blood-brain barrier.
It multiplies only in the liver
Multiplying exclusively in the liver is hepatitis B virus. JC virus is latent in the gut and kidney tubules and, by crossing the blood-brain barrier, destroys myelin-producing cells.

set2.io: 4 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of DNA viruses of medical importance.
set2.q: Which of these DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) virus groups is enveloped?
opts: Poxviruses

Correct. The enveloped DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) viruses are the poxviruses, herpesviruses and hepadnaviruses, all double-stranded. Adenoviruses, polyomaviruses and papillomaviruses are nonenveloped double-stranded, and parvoviruses nonenveloped single-stranded.
Adenoviruses

Adenoviruses are nonenveloped double-stranded DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) viruses. The enveloped groups are poxviruses, herpesviruses and hepadnaviruses. To tell them apart: no nonenveloped group appears on the enveloped list.
Papillomaviruses

Papillomaviruses are nonenveloped double-stranded DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) viruses, listed with adenoviruses and polyomaviruses. Poxviruses carry an envelope. To tell them apart: papillomaviruses sit on the nonenveloped list.
Parvoviruses

Parvoviruses are nonenveloped and single-stranded. The enveloped DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) viruses are poxviruses, herpesviruses and hepadnaviruses. To tell them apart: the single-stranded group is also nonenveloped.

set2.io: 4 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of DNA viruses of medical importance.
set2.q: The purple lesions shown are Kaposi sarcoma in the mouth of a patient with acquired immunodeficiency syndrome. Beyond the skin and mouth, where may this tumor spread?
opts: Along a single dermatome

A band of vesicles along one dermatome is shingles, reactivated varicella zoster virus following a sensory nerve. Kaposi sarcoma is not confined to a nerve path; it may disseminate to internal organs.
To the retina, with blind spots
Retinitis with blind spots is cytomegalovirus disease in acquired immunodeficiency syndrome. The spread described for Kaposi sarcoma is dissemination from the skin to internal organs.
Into the jaw, swelling the cheek
A tumor that develops in the jaw and grossly swells the cheek is Burkitt lymphoma, from Epstein-Barr virus, in central African children. Kaposi sarcoma may disseminate to internal organs.
To internal organs

Correct. Kaposi sarcoma, linked with human herpesvirus 8, appears as small, painless, discolored lumps on the skin, but it may disseminate to internal organs. Human herpesvirus 8 spreads through saliva, sexual contact, blood transfusion and organ transplant.

set2.io: 2 — Compare and contrast the characteristics of a lytic viral infection versus a persistent chronic or persistent latent infection.
set2.q: A man who had chickenpox as a child develops the painful rash shown. Where had the virus been latent?
opts: In B lymphocytes
B cells are where Epstein-Barr virus lies dormant before it is reactivated. Varicella zoster virus waits in neurons of a nerve ganglion, which is why shingles follows a nerve pathway.
In the salivary glands
The salivary glands are infected by cytomegalovirus, the salivary gland virus, and by Epstein-Barr virus. Shingles comes from varicella zoster virus reactivating in neurons of a nerve ganglion.
In the kidney and bladder lining

The kidney and the lining of the ureters and bladder are where BK polyomavirus lies dormant. Varicella zoster virus is latent in neurons of a ganglion and travels down the sensory nerve when it reactivates.
In neurons of a nerve ganglion

Correct. After primary chickenpox, varicella zoster virus enters neurons and remains latent. Activated in the ganglion, for example by stress, it migrates down the sensory nerve to the skin and causes shingles, with inflammation of the ganglion and pain down the nerve pathway.

set2.q: What seems to be the primary reservoir of cowpox infection?
opts: Humans
Humans are the only host of variola, the smallpox virus. Human cowpox infections are rare and come from animals; the primary reservoir appears to be rodents.
Sheep and goats
Sheep and goats are the ruminant hosts of orf virus, a parapox virus that causes sore mouth. Cowpox's primary reservoir appears to be rodents.
Rodents

Correct. Despite its name, cowpox is found not only in cows but in rodents, cats and zoo animals, and rodents seem to be its primary reservoir. Humans can catch it from rodents by handling cats that interacted with them.
Cows
Cows gave the disease its name, but cowpox is found in rodents, cats and zoo animals too, and rodents seem to be the primary reservoir. The name is a trap, not the reservoir.

set2.io: 1 — Recall the steps of DNA virus replication.
set2.q: Where in the host cell do herpesviruses replicate?
opts: Free in the cytoplasm

Most ribonucleic acid (RNA) viruses multiply in and are released from the cytoplasm. Herpesviruses carry double-stranded deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA), and like most deoxyribonucleic acid viruses they replicate within the nucleus.
At the cell membrane, while budding
Budding through a cell membrane is how an enveloped animal virus is released and gets its envelope, after replication is finished. Herpesvirus replication itself happens within the nucleus.
Within the nucleus

Correct. Herpesviruses replicate within the host cell nucleus, as most deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) viruses do; most deoxyribonucleic acid viruses are budded off the nucleus. During latency their deoxyribonucleic acid also stays in the nucleus, as an episome.
In cytoplasmic factory areas

Multiplying in cytoplasmic factory areas is the exception of the poxviruses, the largest and most complex animal viruses. Herpesviruses are deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) viruses that follow the usual pattern and replicate within the nucleus.
